hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — HELD 82%
hypotheses.d: HELD. The promised authenticated footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders still has not landed, so the falsifier remains un-run. The week was IRGC-forward — the Guard, not the foreign ministry, confirmed it ran the Oman channel and announced the revenue-sharing terms, and the Guard made the mine-strike claim — but that is DENIED as a raise under the shared-prediction rule: 'the Guard runs the maritime file' is predicted just as strongly by an ordinary reading in which the IRGC is a powerful institution under a functioning Supreme Leader, which is a much weaker claim than 'the IRGC rules Iran'. The 82% cap stands for exactly the reason it was set.

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Held at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: Nobody's hurrying on Hormuz — 60% → 65% (RAISED)
hypotheses.d: Its first fact that BEATS a rival instead of merely fitting itself. On 30 Aug the US struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak after observing Guard personnel preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the strait — two days after CENTCOM declared the lanes fully cleared, and while Muscat negotiates a minesweeping calendar. The 08-30 audit had installed a genuine rival — a physical clock, minesweeping simply takes time — and ruled this hypothesis must beat it. A physical clock runs down; this one is being rewound, by the exact actor the hypothesis named in advance. Capped at +5 on three counts kept in front: CENTCOM is the interested party and 'observed preparations' is unpublished intelligence used to justify a strike; Al Jazeera published a technical challenge on 31 Aug to whether Iran can even mine by rocket as claimed; and IRGC counter-coercion against a blockade that has redirected 83 vessels, disabled three and boarded two explains the same act without any rent motive. Not pre-event.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — HELD 60%, tell sharpened
hypotheses.d: August continues the signature: 125 PLA aerial ADIZ incursions (the 2026 decline intact) against 152 non-warship PRC vessels in the first 21 days, ~60% coast guard, with the east-of-Taiwan patrols now a declared 'new normal'. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up. NOT moved — this is the same signal that bought +5 on 08-26, and re-marking on the continuation of its own evidence is the double-count the audit named. The important item is against my own test: if Beijing has DECLARED the patrols permanent, their persistence through the Sept 24 visit is close to uninformative. Re-specified now, in advance and stricter — the informative observation on 09-23→09-25 is a boarding, an inspection, or a first-time-area incursion. Mere presence no longer counts as confirmation.

hypotheses.name: Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it holds at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Falsifiers: token export volumes, Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing not actually swinging off the Middle East, or the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appearing. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Note it is DISTINCT from 'The Portfolio State' below, which is about the vehicle rather than the motive.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — HELD 52%
hypotheses.d: Confirming but shared, therefore ambience: Treasury again held back on Chinese financial institutions, with mainstream reporting now naming the mechanism outright — designating them 'could create tensions before Xi's visit'. Bessent's promised weekly cadence hit banks but no Chinese one, and at the G20 he pushed severing Iran financial ties while China dissented. Both the leverage read and the ordinary 'Washington won't detonate its own summit' read predict all of it. The strongest weekly argument AGAINST, logged rather than absorbed: the US struck Iran on three consecutive nights and took Iranian fire onto three Arab host states. Deliberate slow-walking for leverage sits badly with sustained kinetic escalation that raises the cost of the thing being slow-walked — that counterweight is what holds the number at 52.

hypotheses.name: A pre-announcement leak into oil futures — 40% → 34% (biggest mover)
hypotheses.d: Its lead conditional has now gone unfired across three weeks containing the most violently market-moving Iran news since April — the 30 Aug Larak strike, three nights of exchanges, two struck VLCCs, Brent to ~$95 — with not one reported nine-figure pre-announcement episode. The file is confirmed as historical and bounded: DOJ is probing four trades totalling ~$2.6bn, all inside a five-week window that closed in April — Mar 23 (>$500m, ~15 min before Trump's delay post), Apr 7 ($960m before the ceasefire), Apr 17 ($760m, ~20 min before Iran said Hormuz was open), Apr 21 ($430m before the extension). CORRECTION BANKED AGAINST THIS ENTRY: the ledger's earlier '~$2.2bn cluster' for Mar 23 and its '~$7bn' aggregate are both withdrawn as over-wide constructions. The cut is made on the hypothesis's own written terms, not on a preferred reading — a conditional set at 60% has burned three of fourteen weeks in the best environment it will ever get and produced nothing. The cut is only −6 because of one genuinely new structural fact: investigators are running a SEPARATE probe into prediction-market activity on the same developments, and the same foreknowledge reaching two unrelated venues is hard to explain as one market-maker hedging client flow. Split now: deliberate leak 34 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 36 / coincidence 10. Still the only entry whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event.

hypotheses.name: NEW · The Portfolio State — coercion converted into sovereign equity, statute retrofitted
hypotheses.d: Strongest form: the US is converting military and sanctions leverage into permanent state equity in strategic supply chains, with the legal authority written to fit transactions rather than the reverse — Venezuela being the first hydrocarbon use of a template already run in chips and critical minerals. The rail predates the headline, which is the only thing licensing a design read at all: Senate NDAA FY2027 §1051 was marked up in MID-JUNE — ten weeks before the 29 Aug deal — creating a DoD Equity Investment Account, authorising OSC equity to $500m and capping any single position at 40% of the entity; the Venezuela stake is 35%, inside a cap that does not legally exist yet. Add DoD's own $400m/15% stake in MP Materials with 100% offtake (structurally identical to Venezuela's '20% of output at cost'), House Oversight already demanding an accounting of Venezuelan oil revenue on 23 Feb, and CFR's tally of 26 government equity deals worth ~$23.9bn. It opens at only 25% because the boring, incompetence and patronage readings are all strong: think tanks have been publicly naming and counting this pattern since 2025 (a policy, not a plot); the Pentagon's own spokesman flatly DENIES that OSC takes equity while WSJ reports it doing so, which is improvisation not design; and a 100-year concession over 65bn bbl routed to one politically connected operator with no published contract is better explained as spoils allocation. Above all the base rate is enormous — Anglo-Persian 1914, the RFC, GM/Chrysler 2009 — so the design premium must be small. NOT a conspiracy claim and must never be scored as one: it requires no secrecy at all, only anticipation, and the honest gap is that I cannot name the operator who executes the warrants. Key test: does the ENACTED NDAA widen §1051 beyond critical minerals to energy, or raise the cap, by 31 Dec (45%)? Scope enacted unchanged kills the design read.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 25% → 22% (CUT, sixth session running)
hypotheses.d: The week finally produced Russia-Iran material and it is the wrong KIND. Moscow said publicly on 01 Sep that air defence is the main focus of military-technical cooperation with Iran, alongside a reported 500 Verba MANPADS and 2,500 missiles and continued fighter deliveries. That is the resupply leg — already priced at 7/10 under 'means'. It moves nothing: it is announced by TASS, an interested party publishing its own helpfulness and the structural opposite of a covert channel; the opportunism branch predicts arms sales to a client at war identically, so under the standing rule it is ambience; and after six sessions there is still ZERO documentary evidence Moscow has influenced Tehran's negotiating position, which is the actual claim. Arms transfers are not persuasion. Cut rather than held because a decay rule that bites only on its deadline is a cliff, not decay. Clock unchanged: 15% on 30 Sep absent documentary evidence, retire below 10%.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Nothing resolved this week, and one file addition cuts against it: the summit's Iran content is now openly reported as an explicit US ask — Chinese pressure on Tehran to reopen the strait — with Beijing expected to want Taiwan concessions in return. An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: Oil hits $108 and the 30-year Treasury yield tops a 2007 high
brief.h: Brent settled $107.63 and the long bond went to 5.36 per cent on the same afternoon - the one combination that says the central bank is not coming.
brief.t: Most days oil and bonds trade against each other: an energy shock scares growth, money runs into Treasuries, yields fall. Tonight they went up together. Brent settled $107.63, up 6.3 per cent and the highest since May; the US ten-year hit 4.95 per cent, the highest since 2023; the thirty-year printed 5.36 per cent, a level last seen in 2007. That pairing is not a mood, it is a message about who is expected to pay. When a lender demands more yield in the same hour that the input cost of everything jumps, the lender is saying he does not expect the Federal Reserve to ease into it - and a government refinancing its cheap 2021-22 borrowing into a five-per-cent long end is doing so at the worst possible moment. The retail evidence has already arrived: producer prices rose 5.4 per cent on the year with the increase concentrated in diesel and heating fuel, the national diesel average crossed $6.00 a gallon for the first time, and the thirty-year mortgage printed 7.07 per cent.
brief.context: Rail and epoch: this is Epoch 7 in the deep-time map, weaponised settlement, running on an Epoch 1 chassis. The 1973-74 architecture yoked oil to the dollar and recycled the surplus into Treasuries; the standing consequence is that an oil shock does not arrive at a sovereign as a headline, it arrives as an inflation term inside every long discount rate. The desk that decides is not the podium - it is the FOMC on 16 September, where three members already dissented FOR a hike in July, and the primary dealers who must absorb the coupon supply. The mechanism to hold is the supply-shock trap: the policy rate is a demand instrument, and pointing it at a refining and shipping constraint buys a recession without much disinflation, which is why Blinder and Bernanke concluded central banks have generally been right to look through energy shocks. Base rate and the difference that matters: in 1973-74 Arthur Burns looked through and America got embedded inflation; in 1979-80 Volcker did not and America got two recessions plus a restored currency - two data points, opposite errors, which is exactly why this desk holds a 65 per cent question rather than a 90 per cent one. The influence map runs principal (a Treasury facing a rollover calendar) to agent (the FOMC) to operator (the SOMA desk still buying bills) to market (the thirty-year) to target (every household repricing a mortgage at 7.07). Falsifier: if the thirty-year retreats below 5.25 while Brent holds above $105, the long end was pricing fiscal supply rather than the oil shock, and the through-line in this card is wrong.

consp.claim: On /biz/ the loudest threads say $150 oil is already locked in - one cites a Jim Cramer clip as the signal, which the board is reading as a contrary indicator - while a separate thread titled 'THIS IS NOT A DRILL' tells readers to exit all markets and buy guns, gold and canned food. Alongside them a thread asks what a promised $5,000-per-adult payment would do to the ten- and thirty-year yield, treating the transfer and the long end as one story.
consp.spread: Multiple /biz/ threads through the day, the largest running several hundred replies; the diesel record has its own all-caps thread.
consp.read: The frame is capitulation-to-catastrophe, and it maps onto a mechanism this desk genuinely tracks: a fiscal transfer priced into the long end is the fiscal-dominance rhyme, and the boards got there before most columnists did. The checkable kernel is narrow - whether a $5,000 transfer exists as a bill with a pay-for, and whether the thirty-year holds 5.25 - and the part that is not checkable is the number 150, which this desk now scores openly at 52 per cent rather than asserting. Note the inversion tell: when a television personality is being cited as proof, the argument has moved from supply to sentiment.

angles.party: Energy producers and the states that tax them
angles.effect: A 75 per cent year-to-date rise in crude is the largest transfer to producers since 2022
Diesel has no substitute on a six-month horizon, so the cost passes straight through to shipped goods
Borrows into a 5.36 per cent long end while refinancing the 2021-22 low-rate vintage
A 7.07 per cent mortgage is the oil shock arriving as a monthly payment

dec.kill: If core producer prices stay near 0.2 per cent monthly while headline runs hot, the shock is still energy rather than general inflation, and the case for tightening into it weakens rather than strengthens.

brief.head: Iran strikes a US drone boat as Trump rules out any deal
brief.h: The IRGC says it hit an American unmanned surface vessel in the strait, four projectiles struck two ships off Oman, and the president told a party convention he is not interested in negotiating.
brief.t: Notice what was and was not hit. Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they struck a US Saildrone-type unmanned vessel in the Strait of Hormuz; the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reported four projectiles hitting two vessels near Khasab, on Oman's side, with fires aboard. The unmanned part is the whole point. A crewless platform is a rung on the escalation ladder with the human cost engineered out, which means each side can answer the last move without producing the one thing that forces a decision - a body. That is why this desk's risk gate is written in crew and flag rather than in hulls or headlines, and why it stayed shut tonight. The second half of the day is what moved the odds: speaking at the Republican midterm convention, the president said there is 'a little activity at Pickaxe' - the buried tunnel complex near Natanz - advised Tehran 'not to get cute', and said he is not interested in negotiating.
brief.context: Constraint before character: neither principal is boxed into a campaign tonight, but both are boxed out of a deal. Tehran's constraint is that the Guards have staked an institutional claim on administering the strait, so any settlement that drops the toll costs them the asset the war produced; Washington's is a midterm calendar in which US officials have framed secondary sanctions as the plan until after November. The desk that decides is CENTCOM and the National Security Council, not the convention stage. The framework is Schelling twice over: first leaving-something-to-chance, where an unmanned collision surface generates incidents neither side chose, and second commitment, where a public red line plus a public claim the line is being crossed raises the reputational cost of inaction. The base rate cuts against alarm - militarised interstate disputes escalate to war in low single-digit percentages and none initiated since 2001 has - but this board deliberately does NOT use that class, because the correct reference class is recurrence of an already-resumed campaign, where Fortna's work on ceasefires lacking an agreed verifier puts breakdown rates far higher. Influence map: principal Tehran's security establishment, agent the IRGC navy, operator the units running the restricted zone that begins at the US blockade line, market the war-risk underwriters, target the crews of neutral hulls. Incompetence alternative, named as required: a drone struck near a blockade line may be a local commander's engagement rather than a national decision, and the difference is invisible from outside. Falsifier for tonight's raise: fourteen days with no strike on an Iranian state target returns this to 51 and scores the move a miss.

consp.claim: The long-running /pol/ Persia-Israel general is headed 'Day 195 of the 4-Day Special Military Operation to Regime Change Iran', alongside 'Day 1069' of a campaign in Lebanon billed as two days - the running joke being that the advertised length was the lie that sold the war. A separate strand argues the drone-boat episode is staged by one side or the other, offered as proof depending on which state media the poster distrusts more.
consp.spread: The general thread runs continuously at several hundred replies per iteration and was the board's largest geopolitical thread today.
consp.read: Strip the sneer and there is a real analytical claim underneath, and it is one the strategist canon endorses: a war sold as weeks that runs months is simultaneously a planning failure and evidence about who actually holds the file. Score both. The staged-drone strand is the unfalsifiable half - neither IRGC footage nor CENTCOM silence settles it - which is precisely why this desk's gate is a crewed hull and a named casualty rather than any image.

angles.effect: A strike on an unmanned American vessel is a demonstration with no US funeral attached - maximum signal, minimum trigger
A Pickaxe warning delivered to a party convention plays to a domestic audience without committing an interagency timetable
Kuwait, Bahrain, the UAE and Oman absorb the incidents and the insurance costs without a vote on the escalation
Pay the war-risk premium whichever way the claim about the drone is resolved

dec.kill: Published imagery or a CENTCOM confirmation of a captured or destroyed US unmanned vessel would move this from claim to fact; a US-flagged merchant hull struck, or an American killed, is what moves this board's risk state.

brief.head: Saudi Arabia's Hormuz bypass now exits through a Houthi-held strait
brief.h: The East-West pipeline was built so Saudi crude could avoid Hormuz, but the barrels it carries leave at Yanbu and most of them must still pass Bab el-Mandeb.
brief.t: Here is the sentence that explains tonight's oil price better than any missile count: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline running at full capacity is the reason crude is not already at $150. The Petroline crosses the kingdom from the Gulf to the Red Sea and hit a record seven million barrels a day in March, roughly two million of it feeding domestic refineries and the rest loading at Yanbu, which handled 92 per cent of Saudi seaborne crude exports in June. The trouble is arithmetic, not ideology: between 70 and 75 per cent of what leaves Yanbu has to go south through Bab el-Mandeb to reach Asia or Europe. So the bypass built to defeat one chokepoint terminates at another - and this week Ansar Allah took Mocha and Zuqar island and put a hostile force on the eastern bank of a strait twenty-nine kilometres wide. A threat you can shoot down is a toll. A force on the bank is a door.
brief.context: Epoch and rail: Epoch 1, oil yoked to the dollar, whose physical leg is the guarantee that Gulf barrels reach buyers. The Petroline is itself the rail that predates this headline - built in the 1980s precisely against an Iranian strait closure - which is why a design read here is about ARCHITECTURE rather than timing: the pipeline was planned against Hormuz and nobody planned its exit against Yemen. The desk that decides is not Riyadh's information ministry but Aramco's shipping department and the Lloyd's Joint War Committee, which prices the strait. The mechanism is Hirschman on substitutability - leverage comes from whether an alternative can physically reach the market, not from volume - and the base rate should chill: the Suez Canal, shut in 1967 when a land power held one bank, did not reopen until 1975, and clearing it took about a year after the political decision. Missile campaigns run in weeks; bank-held waterways run in years. Influence map: principal Ansar Allah and its Iranian sponsor, operator the shore battery and the underwriter, market the war-risk quote, target Egypt, whose Suez receipts are a top-three hard-currency earner under an IMF programme. Falsifier and the honest counterweight: if weekly transits recover toward the 273-a-week baseline within a fortnight and war-risk quotes keep carving Saudi-linked tonnage out separately, Mocha bought position rather than closure and this card overstates it.

consp.claim: A large /pol/ thread declares in all caps that the Houthis have just blown up the Saudi East-West pipeline and that the oil market is about to go vertical. A parallel /biz/ thread argues Hormuz traffic never recovered after the announced ceasefire and that the market is only now admitting the barrels are not coming.
consp.spread: Over two hundred replies on /pol/ within the day; the Hormuz-traffic claim recurs across several /biz/ market threads.
consp.read: The pipeline claim is carried by no wire and should be treated as unsupported until one carries it - but it is not invented from nothing, which is the interesting part. Houthi forces did claim strikes on Aramco facilities at Jizan and Yanbu in July and August, and at Yanbu two ballistic missiles were intercepted by a Patriot battery operated in the kingdom by the Greek military. So the board has taken a real and repeatedly attempted target and promoted an attempt into an accomplished fact - the ordinary mechanism by which rumour outruns reporting in a fog. The checkable kernel is specific and public: Petroline throughput, and whether Aramco declares force majeure at Yanbu. The /biz/ traffic claim is closer to right than most headlines: transits fell from thirty on Wednesday to twelve on Thursday.

brief.head: Putin lands in Delhi as BRICS prepares to switch on a payment rail
brief.h: The 18th BRICS summit opens on 12 September with Putin and Xi in the room and one deliverable that would actually matter: an operating link between the Russian, Chinese, Indian and Brazilian payment systems.
brief.t: Ignore the currency talk; watch the plumbing. India has explicitly ruled out a common BRICS currency and its foreign minister has said there is no policy of replacing the dollar, so the summit's headline cannot be the thing everyone argues about. The deliverable that would matter is BRICS Pay - an interoperability layer linking Russia's SPFS, China's CIPS, India's UPI and Brazil's Pix - targeted for operational deployment at this summit, alongside a piloted trade-settlement token reported as backed 40 per cent by gold and 60 per cent by a basket of member currencies. The distinction is the whole story. A currency is a political project that requires members to give something up. A payment rail is an engineering project that lets them keep everything and route around one specific vulnerability: the correspondent banking system through which dollar access can be switched off. Putin arrived Friday for a three-day visit, his first overseas BRICS appearance since February 2022 - which tells you which member most wants the rail finished.
brief.context: Epoch 7, weaponised settlement, and the rail that predates the headline is the 2022 freezing of Russian central-bank reserves, which taught every surplus state that Treasuries are political objects. This is the unit front of the conflict tree - what invoices energy and debt - and the correct desk is not the leaders' plenary but the central banks that would have to publish interoperability standards and carry settlement risk. The base rate is the discipline: BRICS communiques have promised local-currency settlement at essentially every summit since 2011 and produced declarations rather than operating rails, so the outside view on 'this time the document means something' is low. The falsifiable test this desk publishes and will score: does the New Delhi declaration name a specific rail, a named settlement asset, and a DATED interoperability pilot with participating central banks - or does it endorse the principle again. The second-order effect to watch is not the dollar's share of reserves, which moves in decades, but insurance and shipping documentation, because that is where sanctioned trade actually binds. Incompetence alternative: three of the four systems being linked run incompatible messaging standards with domestic regulators who have not agreed liability, which is the boring reason such projects slip.

consp.claim: Ahead of every recent BRICS summit a claim circulates in /biz/ precious-metals threads and across X that the bloc is about to announce a gold-backed currency that ends dollar dominance; this cycle it has attached itself to reporting of the 40-per-cent-gold settlement token.
consp.spread: Recurrent in the /pmg/ and /XSG/ generals on /biz/ and heavily syndicated by crypto-adjacent news aggregators.
consp.read: This is the most reliably recurring forecast in the retail macro world and it has been wrong before every summit since 2023, which makes it a useful calibration marker rather than a threat. The kernel that IS real is the token pilot and the New Development Bank's reported agreement in principle - but a trade-settlement token used between consenting exporters is not a reserve currency, and conflating them is the move to watch. The persuasion technique is the category slide: a narrow, technical, opt-in instrument described in the vocabulary of a universal one.

brief.head: Pentagon moves to lend $5bn to an AI cloud startup
brief.h: The Office of Strategic Capital is in talks to lend roughly $5 billion to Fluidstack for data-centre supply chain and component manufacturing, with Palmer Luckey's Erebor Bank advising the application.
brief.t: Read this next to the thirty-year yield and it stops being a technology story. The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital - the same desk that took an equity position in a Venezuelan oil venture earlier this cycle - is in talks to lend about $5 billion to Fluidstack, not to build an AI facility but to shore up the American supply chain and manufacturing capacity for data-centre components. The application is being advised by Erebor Bank, the hard-tech national bank Palmer Luckey opened in February, which has already gathered more than $4.6 billion in deposits. Follow the money and the shape is familiar: when private credit will not fund a strategic input at a price the state finds acceptable, the state becomes the lender and calls it industrial policy. What makes it notable tonight is the cost of funds - the sovereign doing the lending is itself borrowing thirty-year money at 5.36 per cent, the highest since 2007. That is the definition of a subsidy, and somebody is paying it.
brief.context: Epoch 7 again, but on the priority front rather than the unit front: who gets paid first when a credit cycle turns. The rail that predates this headline is real and dated - the Office of Strategic Capital was created in 2022 with explicit loan and loan-guarantee authorities for critical technologies, so a state-credit facility for compute is an activation of an existing statute rather than an invention, which is what licenses a design read about ARCHITECTURE while forbidding one about timing. The desk that decides is OSC's credit committee and the appropriators who set its authority, not the Secretary's podium. The mechanism to hold is state credit as pre-positioning: governments finance the input they expect to be scarce in a conflict, as they did with shipping in 1916 and synthetic rubber in 1942. The base rate is sobering in both directions - sovereign industrial-credit programmes produced both the Reconstruction Finance Corporation and a long tail of losses, and recovery rates on directed lending into a boom sector are historically poor. Falsifier for the sceptical read: if the loan closes with collateral over physical plant and a component offtake schedule, this is supply-chain finance and behaves like it; if it closes as unsecured credit against compute revenue, it is a balance-sheet transfer into an asset class the private market is already crowding.

consp.claim: The circulating reading is that this is an AI bailout wearing a defence uniform - that private credit has stopped underwriting data-centre buildout at acceptable terms and the state has stepped in to keep the capex cycle alive. The sharper version notes that the bank advising the loan was founded by a defence contractor and treats the arrangement as the military-tech stack financing itself.
consp.spread: Amplified on X, where a member of Congress called the report 'absolutely terrifying' and a prominent AI critic mocked it, against investor accounts telling readers to calm down; picked up across tech aggregators the same evening.
consp.read: The bailout frame is a hypothesis with a checkable test rather than a slur, and the test is the collateral: rescue finance is unsecured and backward-looking, supply-chain finance is secured against plant and tied to deliveries. What it is downstream of matters too - the frame rides a broader argument about whether AI capex is credit-funded, which this desk tracks separately. The overlap with the record is real: OSC's authorities and the Venezuela stake are documented. The gap is that nothing published yet shows distress at Fluidstack, and 'the state is lending' is not the same claim as 'the borrower could not otherwise borrow'.

angles.effect: Sovereign credit at below-market terms de-risks a capital-intensive buildout
Buys domestic component capacity without an appropriation for a facility
Compete against a borrower with a government cost of funds
Carries the credit risk while the sovereign itself borrows long at 5.36 per cent

dec.kill: The terms sheet. Secured against physical plant with a component offtake schedule and this is industrial policy; unsecured against compute revenue and the bailout reading gains.

watch: The word UNMANNED in every report of tonight's Hormuz strike. As long as the platforms being hit have no crew, both sides retain a rung they can keep climbing; the first crewed American hull or American casualty is the variable that has historically moved US decisions, and it is the only thing that moves this board's risk state.

Petroline throughput and any Aramco force-majeure notice at Yanbu or Jizan. The East-West pipeline running full is the analytically load-bearing reason crude is at $108 rather than higher, and it is the least-covered number on the board.

The war-risk quotation at Bab el-Mandeb, and specifically whether it still carves out Saudi-linked tonnage separately from general trade. A strait closes by quotation before it closes by minefield, and weekly transits against the 273-a-week baseline are the public proxy.

The FOMC statement language on 16 September rather than the rate. The European Central Bank raised this week and said explicitly that it is preparing for longer-lasting inflation; whether the Fed keeps its look-through sentence is the observable GEO-029 turns on, and three meetings remain in the window.

The New Delhi declaration text on 12-13 September: does BRICS Pay get a named rail, a named settlement asset and a dated interoperability pilot with participating central banks, or does the document endorse the principle again. India has already ruled out a common currency, so the principle is not the test.

The Fluidstack terms sheet if the loan closes. Secured against physical plant with a component offtake schedule is industrial policy; unsecured against compute revenue is a balance-sheet transfer, and the two imply very different things about private credit's appetite for AI buildout.
lesson: Today's lesson is the oldest trap in central banking, and both ways out of it are bad. Call it the SUPPLY-SHOCK TRAP: an interest rate is a demand instrument - it works by making people borrow and spend less - and it has no ability whatever to produce a barrel of diesel or reopen a strait. So when prices rise because the supply of something is physically constrained, a central bank that tightens is applying the wrong tool, buying a recession in exchange for very little disinflation; and a central bank that does nothing risks the price rise migrating into wages and expectations, where it stops being about oil and becomes self-sustaining. Economics has one clean example of each error. Arthur Burns looked through the 1973-74 oil shock and America got a decade of embedded inflation; Paul Volcker refused to look through the 1979 shock and America got two recessions and a restored currency. Alan Blinder and Ben Bernanke, reviewing the record, concluded that on balance central banks have been RIGHT to look through supply shocks - which is why this desk holds the probability of a Federal Reserve hike by December at 65 per cent rather than at 90, even with producer prices running 5.4 per cent and diesel through $6 a gallon. Here is what the framework actually predicts, and it is testable next Wednesday: watch whether the FOMC statement still describes energy-driven inflation as something it expects to pass through, or drops that language the way the European Central Bank did this week when it raised rates and said out loud that it is preparing for LONGER-LASTING inflation. The language is the decision; the rate move only confirms it.

events.label: Strait of Hormuz
events.note: The IRGC says it struck a US Saildrone-type unmanned surface vessel inside what Tehran calls a restricted zone beginning at the American blockade line. Transits ran at seven on 9 September against a pre-war baseline near 130 a day.

events.label: Khasab, Oman
events.note: UKMTO reported four projectiles striking two vessels near Khasab with fires aboard. Neither is reported as US-flagged, which is why this desk's risk gate did not move.

events.label: Pickaxe Mountain / Natanz
events.note: The president said 'a little activity' has been observed at the buried tunnel complex and advised Tehran not to get cute. A stated red line plus a claim it is being crossed is a commitment mechanism, not a prediction of a strike.

events.label: Mocha
events.note: Ansar Allah took the last government-held Red Sea port south of Hodeidah, with government units withdrawing south to Dhubab. More than 500 dead and nearly 20,000 displaced since the offensive resumed.

events.label: Bab el-Mandeb
events.note: Transits fell from thirty on Wednesday to twelve on Thursday. The strait is 29km at its narrowest and now has a hostile force on its eastern bank rather than merely within missile range of it.

events.label: Yanbu
events.note: Terminus of the East-West pipeline and the outlet for 92 per cent of Saudi seaborne crude in June; 70-75 per cent of what loads here must pass Bab el-Mandeb. Houthi missiles aimed at installations here were intercepted in July.

events.label: Jazan
events.note: The 400,000 b/d Aramco complex, roughly a tenth of company net refining, reported hit and shut repeatedly since late July. This is the asset converting a Yemeni land war into a global diesel price.

events.label: Ali al-Taher ridge
events.note: Israel says it demolished a two-kilometre Hezbollah tunnel system in Nabatieh with enough explosive to register a 4.1 tremor, declaring operational control above and below ground. A capstone reads as consolidation, not necessarily as prelude.

events.label: Pokrovsk axis
events.note: Still the most active direction on the front, with Ukraine's general staff reporting the largest share of daily clashes here. Autumn rasputitsa is the seasonal variable behind this board's Q4 tempo question.

events.label: New Delhi
events.note: Putin arrived Friday for a three-day visit; Xi joins for the 18th BRICS summit on 12-13 September. The deliverable to score is whether BRICS Pay gets a dated interoperability pilot or another endorsement of the principle.

events.label: Lima
events.note: Peru joined the US-led counter-narcotics coalition during Rubio's Andean tour, while Rubio pledged Washington would not act unilaterally against traffickers despite recent strikes.

fired: RISK GATE - NEAREST APPROACH YET, AND STILL NOT FIRED. The published gate is a struck US-flagged merchant hull or a confirmed American death. quiz.q: The brief argues that oil and long-term bond yields rising on the SAME day is diagnostic. What does that combination signal?
options: That investors expect an imminent recession, which is why they are selling oil
That lenders do not expect the central bank to ease into the shock, so they demand more yield rather than rushing into Treasuries
That the Treasury has cancelled its long-bond auctions
That the dollar is being abandoned as a reserve currency
quiz.why: Normally an energy shock scares growth, money runs into government bonds and yields FALL. When yields rise alongside crude, the bond market is saying it expects no rescue and is pricing inflation into every long discount rate instead. That is the tape the plumbing lens treats as a signature, not a mood.

quiz.q: Why does the brief treat Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as central to tonight's oil price?
options: It carries Iranian crude to market under a permit arrangement
It was damaged this week, removing 7 million barrels a day from supply
It bypasses the Strait of Hormuz, but the barrels it carries still leave by sea at Yanbu and mostly pass through Bab el-Mandeb
It is the only pipeline capable of carrying heavy crude to Gulf Coast refiners
quiz.why: The pipeline is the reason analysts say crude is not already at $150 - it routes around one chokepoint. But a pipeline ends at a port, and 70 to 75 per cent of what loads at Yanbu must transit Bab el-Mandeb, where a hostile force now holds the eastern bank. A bypass with a besieged exit is not a bypass.

quiz.q: The brief makes a point of the word UNMANNED in tonight's Hormuz strike. Why does it matter analytically?
options: Unmanned vessels are not covered by maritime law, so the attack was legal
It means the attack was probably fabricated
A platform with no crew gives both sides a rung on the escalation ladder that does not produce the casualty which forces a decision
Unmanned vessels are cheaper, so the economic damage was small
quiz.why: The cost of an exchange is what disciplines it. Remove the crew and you remove the funeral, the domestic outrage and the political requirement to answer - so the exchange can continue without either side choosing a campaign. That is why this desk's risk gate is written in crew and flag rather than in incident counts.

quiz.q: According to the brief, what is the actual test of whether the BRICS summit in Delhi matters?
options: Whether the members announce a gold-backed common currency
Whether the declaration names a specific payment rail, a named settlement asset and a DATED central-bank pilot
Whether Putin and Xi appear together in public
Whether India agrees to stop buying discounted Russian crude
quiz.why: India has explicitly ruled out a common currency, so that cannot be the test. A currency requires members to give something up; a payment rail lets them keep everything and route around the correspondent banking system where dollar access can be switched off. Declarations promising local-currency settlement have appeared at nearly every summit since 2011 - only a dated, named pilot distinguishes this one.

quiz.q: CRITICAL THINKING. A post reads: 'The Houthis just blew up the Saudi East-West pipeline. Oil is going vertical.' No wire is reporting it. Which observable is the best test?
options: Whether the claim is being repeated by many accounts, since volume indicates credibility
Whether oil futures rise in the next hour, since the market would know first
Published Petroline throughput figures and whether Aramco declares force majeure at Yanbu
Whether the Houthis deny it, since a denial would confirm the strike
quiz.why: Spread measures belief, not truth, and a price move is compatible with the rumour itself moving the market. The claim is not invented from nothing - Houthi forces did claim strikes on Aramco sites at Jizan and Yanbu in July and August, with missiles at Yanbu intercepted - so this is an attempt promoted into an accomplishment. The honest test is the physical record: throughput, and whether the seller tells its buyers it cannot deliver.

sections.t: US diesel set an all-time record this week at $5.820 a gallon, and the crack spread — the refiner's fee for turning crude into something an engine can burn — printed an all-time $108 a barrel while Brent sat at an unremarkable $96. In the same week US missiles reportedly struck a tanker at Iran's Kharg Island anchorage, and Ukrainian drones held Russian refinery runs at 3.6m barrels a day, the lowest since May 2002.

Crude — the thing everyone photographs and embargoes — is behaving; refined product is not. A $108 crack means the market will pay more to convert a barrel than the barrel is worth: a fact about cokers and hydrotreaters, not about oil. Name the mechanism — the conversion bottleneck. The binding constraint is never the abundant input but the narrow step in the middle, which cannot be built on the timescale of a war or an election.

sections.h: Deep history I — Rockefeller never wanted the oil
sections.t: John D. Rockefeller owned almost no wells. He owned the refineries of Cleveland, and what he did with them in 1871 is the founding text of chokepoint economics. Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad chartered the South Improvement Company, and Rockefeller's terms inside it were breathtaking: the Erie, New York Central and Pennsylvania would pay the SIC a rebate of $1.06 on every barrel it shipped — and a drawback of $1.06 on every barrel shipped by refiners outside the club. He was paid when his rivals did business. The charter was repealed that April before a single transaction cleared, and Ida Tarbell's exposé later finished the job — but the insight outlived the scandal: crude is worthless until someone converts and moves it, and whoever owns the narrow step prices the wide one.

sections.h: Deep history II — the war decided at the still
sections.t: The largest test of this proposition was the Allied air war, fought inside the alliance before it was fought over Germany. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command believed in punishment: burn the cities, break the will. Carl Spaatz and Arthur Tedder pushed what Harris dismissed as panacea targets — oil. Germany had almost no crude. It had Bergius hydrogenation, synthetic fuel pressed from coal at Leuna, Pölitz and Brüx, plants too enormous to hide. The oil plan began in May 1944. Leuna alone absorbed 22 raids, 6,552 bomber sorties and 18,328 tons of bombs across a year, behind Europe's heaviest flak concentration. It worked anyway. German synthetic output fell from a peak of 316,000 tons a month to 107,000 in June 1944 and 17,000 by September. Aviation gasoline — the specific fraction, not oil in general — went from 175,000 tons in April to 5,000 in September: 97% gone in five months. From May 1944 Germany consumed more than it produced every month, and the stockpile was gone in six.

sections.h: Deep history II — the fuel, not the factories
sections.t: The detail that makes it unforgettable: over the same period Albert Speer drove German tank and aircraft PRODUCTION to its wartime peak. The Reich ended 1944 with more airframes than it could fly and more panzers than it could move — the factories were fine and the fuel was not. The US Strategic Bombing Survey — written by people with every reason to praise bombing in general — judged the oil and transport campaigns decisive and the city campaign not. Japan lost the same way: the July 1941 freeze is remembered as an oil embargo, but the fatal shortage was 100-octane aviation gasoline, a conversion capability Japan could not build.

sections.h: Deep history III — how the West stopped building stills
sections.t: Now the slow part. The last greenfield major refinery built in the United States was Marathon's Garyville, Louisiana: built 1973-76, online 1977, still running at 596,000 barrels a day. Fifty years, no new plants — and the base is now shrinking: about 132 operable refineries in January 2025 against more than 300 in 1981, with roughly 1.235m b/d of distillation capacity removed in seven recent closures and conversions, over 6.5% of the total. All of it while shale made America the largest crude producer in history at 13.86m b/d. The country built the well and stopped building the still. The capacity emigrated rather than vanished — Jamnagar runs 1.24m b/d, Dangote opened at 650,000 and plans 1.4m, China kept building — so the toll moved east and south, to jurisdictions happy to buy discounted sanctioned crude and sell the product back to the people imposing the sanctions.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: In all three cases the scarce thing is the transformation, and transformation capacity is inelastic over any politically relevant horizon: a new crude supplier takes a fortnight, a new hydrocracker takes five years and a billion dollars. Ukraine is now running the 1944 oil plan at a ten-thousandth of the cost, a drone flying 1,550km to Omsk doing what 6,552 B-17 sorties did to Leuna — Pape's denial thesis tested live. It breaks against me here: Germany had no crude and no neutral supplier, Russia has both, and a 24-year low in refining has not stopped Pokrovsk.

sections.h: The adjudication — Yergin and Blas vs Chris Miller
sections.t: THE ADJUDICATION — YERGIN AND BLAS versus CHRIS MILLER Yergin and Blas hold that energy chokepoints self-heal — inventories, bypass and rerouting absorb shocks forecast to be fatal — and they have been right about the barrel, Brent at $96 in a war that curtailed over 11m b/d. Chris Miller's Chip War argues the opposite for inputs that are not fungible: no reserve of fabs, no bypass for EUV, a decade to rebuild. The evidence splits them by step. Yergin and Blas won the crude argument; the crack is the market announcing the win does not survive one step downstream, because there is no strategic reserve of cokers — the US holds hundreds of millions of barrels of crude in the SPR and about a million barrels of distillate in the Northeast reserve, having stockpiled the input it cannot burn. Miller's case is still weaker in oil than in silicon: diesel is shippable in a way a fab's output is not, so refining heals in 12-24 months rather than 12-24 days.

OECD gasoline demand is in structural decline as EVs scale; diesel and jet demand are not, because trucks, ships, aircraft, mining and data-centre backup have no substitute. But a refinery makes every cut at once, so the economics that close Western refineries — falling gasoline — destroy the distillate capacity nobody meant to lose. A trap, not a cycle; confidence high. The bolder call, near 60%: by the mid-2030s the US is at once the world's largest crude exporter and a chronic net importer of middle distillates, and that buys a strategic PRODUCT reserve — legislated storage of diesel and jet, enacted after a winter shortage rather than before one. What keeps this honest is GEO-026: does the US diesel crack settle below $45 before 15 December 2026? It sits at 35%, so the house is 65% on regime rather than outage — and if the crack mean-reverts on the 2022 schedule, this is an elegant story about a spike, published as a miss.
